summary: Staff engineer on the Build Intelligence team: sets technical direction for the remote cache and remote build execution, makes the self-hosted edition easy to run, works with Trace on the span model, and stays at least half in code.
team: Build Intelligence owns the cache, remote execution and build-time analysis. Six engineers, a product manager and a designer, reporting to the engineering manager. Trace and Enterprise are sister teams.
interviewFormat: Recruiter screen (30 min); hiring-manager interview with Dagny Holmqvist (1 hour); take-home of about four hours; system design (60 min); founder conversation. No AI assistants in live rounds.
companyFacts: Remote cache, remote build execution and pipeline tracing for engineering teams
Founded in Toronto in 2019; hubs in Toronto and Lisbon
About 1,900 organisations run roughly 800,000 builds a day through it
Products: Spanforge Cache, Spanforge Trace, the forge command-line tool, editor extensions
Spanforge Enterprise is the self-hosted edition, including sites with no outbound network
Editor extensions for VS Code and the JetBrains IDEs
values: Treat the customer's time as ours
Disagree in the open, then commit
mustHaves: 6+ years building build, continuous integration or developer infrastructure
Remote build execution and content-addressed caching for Bazel, Gradle or Buck2
Operated ClickHouse or a comparable columnar store at scale
OpenTelemetry in depth: collectors, semantic conventions, sampling
Shipped a command-line tool or IDE extension developers use every day
Delivered software customers run themselves, including air-gapped sites
Single sign-on (SAML, OIDC) and role-based access for enterprise customers
Kubernetes operations, including upgrades of stateful workloads
Written technical leadership: RFCs, design reviews, postmortems
On-call and incident ownership against service level objectives
niceToHaves: Conference talks or public writing about build systems
responsibilities: Set technical direction for the cache and remote execution services
Design eviction, invalidation and integrity checks customers can trust
Make self-hosted installs boring: upgrades, backups, sizing
Work with Trace on the span model joining a build action to its pipeline step
Write and review RFCs; keep decisions written down
Share on-call for the hosted service, one week in six
Join design partner calls and read support tickets
Stay hands-on: at least half the time in code
prepNotes: Round: Dagny Holmqvist, Engineering Manager, Build Intelligence; Tue Sep 15, 13:00-14:00 Eastern; experience and judgment, no coding; she judges depth on caching, written leadership and how I handle a bad day.
Tell me about yourself: 20 years; build and release since Brightwater; two monorepo migrations; now Quillhaven, where I lead the platform group of 9; 50% code, 30% design and review, 20% coaching.
Why Spanforge: the tool is the product, not a cost centre; I have built the same three things in-house (cache, tracing, editor tooling) and want to build them once for many teams.
Faster builds: lead with Quillhaven (41 to 14 minutes at p95); mechanism before number; then Marrowgate as the migration story. Do not mix up the Marrowgate and Marrowfield figures.
Remote execution: Marrowgate. The shared worker pool is the story; say what ran where, how workers drained, what broke hermeticity.
Columnar storage: Quillhaven. Span retention and what it cost; schema by action, ordering key, compression; what I would not do again.
Editor integrations and command-line tools: Lanternfish. Latency budget from save to result; first run with no network; why a language server.
Customer-run installs with no network: Marrowfield. The offline bundle, signing, upgrades without a visit; be honest that it was factories, not paying customers.
Rust: Tracewright only, never in paid work. Say so plainly; offer the sampling design as proof I can reason in it.
Single sign-on and access: Quillhaven, the artifact store with per-team quotas. Thin story; keep it to one minute.
Failure: Quillhaven, the poisoned artifact of March 2023. What I missed, how we found it, signed writes afterwards. No blame on the engineer who pushed it.
Conflict: Marrowgate, the mobile group. Trial on their own code, their numbers, their decision. Disagreement with a manager: Pellucid, build versus buy.
Deadline: Driftline, the signing pipeline before the store freeze. Scope cut first, quality never.
On-call and alerting: Pellucid for the pager clean-up; Quillhaven for the availability target and error budget on the artifact store.
Mentoring: Quillhaven promotions, Marrowgate pairing. Open source: Tracewright, how proposals are decided in public.

Answer shape: context, constraint, my decision, trade-off, result, what I would change; two minutes. Why leaving Quillhaven: platform headcount frozen after the reorganisation; I want the tool to be the business.
questionsToAsk: Which fails more often for customers today: a wrong cache hit or a missed one?
How far behind the hosted product do self-hosted customers usually run?
Who decides the span model when Trace and Build Intelligence disagree?
What does a bad on-call week look like on the hosted cache?
How is a staff engineer's time split between code, RFCs and customers here?
What would make you say, six months in, that this hire worked?
